Stryker vehicles are produced by [[General Dynamics Land Systems]]-Canada (GDLS-C) for the [[United States Army]] in a plant in [[London, Ontario]]. It has four-wheel drive (8×4) and can be switched to all-wheel drive (8×8).{{cite web |url= http://www.eaton.com/Eaton/ProductsServices/ProductsbyMarket/Government/Vehicles/MilitaryVehicles/Stryker/index.htm |archive-url= https://archive.today/20130121200803/http://www.eaton.com/Eaton/ProductsServices/ProductsbyMarket/Government/Vehicles/MilitaryVehicles/Stryker/index.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 January 2013 |title=Stryker |publisher=Eaton.com |access-date=9 August 2012}} The Stryker was conceived as a family of vehicles forming the backbone of a new [[Stryker Brigade Combat Team|medium-weight brigade combat team]] (BCT) that was to strike a balance between [[armored brigade combat team]]s (heavy armor) and [[infantry brigade combat team]]s. The service launched the [[Interim Armored Vehicle]] competition, and in 2000, the service selected the LAV III proposed by GDLS and [[General Motors Defense]]. The service named this family of vehicles the "Stryker". Ten [[variants of the Stryker]] were initially conceived, some of which have been upgraded with [[v-hull]]s.{{cite web | last=Rhen | first=Brad |title=56th Stryker Brigade Combat Team Getting Upgraded Strykers |url=https://www.army.mil/article/277459/56th_stryker_brigade_combat_team_getting_upgraded_strykers |website=U.S. Army |access-date=26 January 2025 |date=21 June 2024 }} ==Development history== ===Interim Armored Vehicle competition=== {{main|Interim Armored Vehicle}} In October 1999, [[Chief of Staff of the United States Army|U.S. Army Chief of Staff]] General [[Eric Shinseki]] outlined a transformation plan for the Army that would allow it to adapt to post–[[Cold War]] conditions. The plan, named "Objective Force", would have the army adopt a flexible doctrine that would allow it to deploy quickly, and be equipped for a variety of operations.{{cite web |url=http://www.armedforces-int.com/article/stryker-2.html |title=Stryker |publisher=ArmedForces-int.com |date=6 March 2006 |access-date=4 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140826165436/http://www.armedforces-int.com/article/stryker-2.html |archive-date=26 August 2014 |url-status=dead}} An early phase of the plan called for the introduction of an [[Interim Armored Vehicle]] (IAV), which was intended to fill the capability gap between heavier and heavily armed, but not easily deployable, vehicles, such as the [[M2 Bradley]], and easily deployable vehicles that are lightly armed and protected, such as the [[Humvee]].{{citation |url=http://www.dtic.mil/cgi-bin/GetTRDoc?AD=ADA505224&Location=U2&doc=GetTRDoc.pdf |title=Hell on Wheels: The U.S. Army's Stryker Brigade Combat Team |author=Captain S. Lucas |date=8 February 2005 |pages=1–2 |access-date=18 May 2010 |archive-date=2 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121002093854/http://www.dtic.mil/cgi-bin/GetTRDoc?AD=ADA505224&Location=U2&doc=GetTRDoc.pdf |url-status=dead}} The IAV was intended as an interim vehicle until light air-mobile vehicles from the [[Future Combat Systems Manned Ground Vehicles]] program came online, none of which did before the program was canceled.[http://www.lexingtoninstitute.org/us-army-combat-vehicle-plans-careen-from-heavy-gcv-to-stryker-lite?a=1&c=1171 U.S. Army Combat Vehicle Plans Careen From Heavy GCV To "Stryker Lite"] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140202121146/http://www.lexingtoninstitute.org/us-army-combat-vehicle-plans-careen-from-heavy-gcv-to-stryker-lite?a=1&c=1171 |date=2 February 2014}} – LexingtonInstitute.org, 30 January 2014 ====Team General Dynamics–General Motors==== In February 2000, [[General Dynamics]] and [[General Motors]] announced they were partnering to enter the IAV competition. The agreement built off earlier cooperative effort: In January 1999, [[General Dynamics Land Systems]] (GDLS)–Canada integrated its Low Profile Turret (LPT) onto an [[assault gun]] version of the [[LAV III]].{{cite book |editor1-last=Foss |editor1-first=Christopher F. |editor1-link=Christopher F. Foss |title=Jane's Armour and Artillery 2011–2012 |publisher=Janes Information Group |location=Surrey |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-71062-960-9 |pages=219–221 |edition=32nd |chapter=Reconnaissance Vehicles |url=https://archive.org/details/janesarmourartil0000unse}}{{cite news |last1=Baumgardner |first1=Neil |title=Competitors Line Up for Medium Armored Vehicle |url=https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/A57772946/ITOF?u=wikipedia&sid=bookmark-ITOF&xid=80d5b64d |access-date=18 January 2023 |work=Defense Daily |issue=35 |publisher=Access Intelligence |date=22 November 2022|volume=204 }}{{Dead link|date=November 2025|fix-attempted=yes |url=}} The [[General Motors Defense]]–General Dynamics Land Systems team was awarded the $8 billion contract in November 2000 to produce 2,131 vehicles of a variant of the Canadian LAV III, for equipping six rapid deployment Brigade Combat Teams by 2008. United Defense protested the contract award in December, saying that their proposal cost less than half that of GM–GDLS. The [[General Accounting Office]] rejected the protest in April 2001.{{cite news |title=National Briefing |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/04/10/us/national-briefing.html |access-date=14 August 2018 |work=The New York Times |date=9 April 2001 |archive-date=14 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180814134947/https://www.nytimes.com/2001/04/10/us/national-briefing.html |url-status=live}} [[United States Assistant Secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics, and Technology|U.S. Assistant Secretary of the Army]] Paul J. Hoeper called the IAV "the best off-the-shelf equipment available in the world in this class", though many in the Army openly wondered whether the vehicles were underclassed compared to the vehicles they might face in battle.{{cite news |last1=Myers |first1=Steven Lee |title=Army's Armored Vehicles Are Already Behind Schedule |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/11/18/us/army-s-armored-vehicles-are-already-behind-schedule.html |access-date=19 July 2018 |work=The New York Times |date=18 November 2000 |archive-date=19 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180719203605/https://www.nytimes.com/2000/11/18/us/army-s-armored-vehicles-are-already-behind-schedule.html |url-status=live}} In February 2002, the Army formally renamed the IAV as the "Stryker" after two unrelated U.S. soldiers who posthumously received the [[Medal of Honor]]: Private First Class [[Stuart S. Stryker]], who died in [[World War II]], and Specialist Four [[Robert F. Stryker]], who died in the [[Vietnam War]].[https://archive.today/20120526231814/http://www.army.mil/features/stryker/default.htm "Army Announces Name For Interim Armored Vehicle"]. U.S. Army. Retrieved 15 August 2007. ===Production=== [[File:Stryker by Augustas Didzgalvis.jpg|thumb|The interior of a Stryker IFV]] In 2002, as the Stryker program faced criticism from lawmakers, including former Congressman [[Newt Gingrich]], Pentagon officials mulled reducing the number of planned Stryker Brigade Combat Teams from six to three for a cost savings of $4.5 billion. In October, the Stryker's [[Lockheed C-130 Hercules|C-130]] air mobility was demonstrated for lawmakers at [[Andrews Air Force Base]]. At the [[Association of the United States Army]], Army Chief of Staff Eric Shinseki defended the six-brigade plan and boasted that the C-130 could carry a Stryker "every way but sideways".{{cite news |last1=Shanker |first1=Thom |title=Army Takes on Critics of an Armored Vehicle |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/10/29/us/army-takes-on-critics-of-an-armored-vehicle.html |access-date=5 August 2018 |work=The New York Times |date=29 October 2002 |archive-date=5 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180805112615/https://www.nytimes.com/2002/10/29/us/army-takes-on-critics-of-an-armored-vehicle.html |url-status=live}} Four brigades were funded in the DoD's budget proposal for fiscal year 2004, with Secretary of Defense [[Donald Rumsfeld]] deferring a decision on two additional until July 2003. In May, the Army readied the Stryker for initial operating capability at [[Fort Polk]]. ''The New York Times'' noted the swiftness with which the program had proceeded from its inception in 1999.{{cite news |last1=Shanker |first1=Thom |title=New Armored Vehicle on Path to Approval |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/05/22/us/new-armored-vehicle-on-path-to-approval.html |access-date=5 August 2018 |work=The New York Times |date=22 May 2003 |archive-date=5 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180805114451/https://www.nytimes.com/2003/05/22/us/new-armored-vehicle-on-path-to-approval.html |url-status=live}} In November 2003, 311 Stryker vehicles were deployed in the [[Iraq War]], where they saw mixed success. Never designed for frontline combat, the vehicles were pressed into [[counterinsurgency]] roles for which there was an unmet need.{{cite news |last1=Schmitt |first1=Eric |title=THE STRUGGLE FOR IRAQ: THE MILITARY; Quick-Hitting Brigade Test-Drives a New Army Vehicle in Iraq |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/12/28/world/struggle-for-iraq-military-quick-hitting-brigade-test-drives-new-army-vehicle.html |access-date=5 August 2018 |work=The New York Times |date=28 December 2003 |archive-date=5 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180805160654/https://www.nytimes.com/2003/12/28/world/struggle-for-iraq-military-quick-hitting-brigade-test-drives-new-army-vehicle.html |url-status=live}} Unexpectedly fierce resistance by insurgents prompted field upgrades to the vehicle's armor. To counter the threat of [[rocket-propelled grenade]]s, General Dynamics developed [[slat armor]], which added 5,000 lb (2,270 kg) to the Stryker's total weight. In addition to hindering mobility in the field, the heavy slat armor made transporting the Stryker via C-130 impossible. In February 2005, [[Chief of Staff of the United States Army|Army Chief of Staff]] General [[Peter J. Schoomaker]] told the [[House Armed Services Committee]] that "we're absolutely enthusiastic about what the Stryker has done." However, a leaked U.S. Army report from December 2004 said the Stryker was "effective and survivable only with limitations for use in small-scale contingencies." The report, which drew from feedback from Stryker personnel in [[Mosul]], described a litany of design flaws, and said the effectiveness of the vehicles was "getting worse, not better."{{cite news |last1=Smith |first1=R. Jeffrey |title=Study Faults Army Vehicle |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/articles/A14284-2005Mar30.html?nav=rss_nation/nationalsecurity/military |access-date=19 July 2018 |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=31 March 2005 |archive-date=19 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180719203423/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/articles/A14284-2005Mar30.html?nav=rss_nation%2Fnationalsecurity%2Fmilitary |url-status=live}} The Stryker 105 mm [[M1128 mobile gun system]] (MGS) moved into [[Low rate initial production|low-rate initial production]] in 2005 for evaluation,{{cite web |url=http://www.generaldynamics.com/news/press_releases/2005/NewsRelease%20December%2015,%202005.htm |title=General Dynamics Delivers First Production Stryker MGS Vehicles |access-date=13 July 2008 |publisher=generaldynamics.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090109164217/http://www.generaldynamics.com/news/press_releases/2005/NewsRelease%20December%2015,%202005.htm |archive-date=9 January 2009 |url-status=dead}} and entered full production in 2007.{{cite web |url=http://www.docstoc.com/docs/6501102/Stryker |title=Stryker |access-date=16 April 2015 |publisher=Docstoc.com |archive-date=16 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150416085300/http://www.docstoc.com/docs/6501102/Stryker |url-status=live}} General Dynamics Land Systems-Canada assembles the Stryker for the U.S. Army in a plant in [[London, Ontario]].{{cite web |url=http://www.gdlscanada.com/index.php/about-us/locations |title=Locations |access-date=1 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170323224730/http://www.gdlscanada.com/index.php/about-us/locations |archive-date=23 March 2017 |url-status=dead}} The vehicle is employed in Stryker Brigade Combat Teams, light and mobile units based on the [[brigade combat team]] doctrine that relies on vehicles connected by military [[Command and Control|C4I (Command, Control, Communications, Computers, and Intelligence)]] networks. General Dynamics's Robotic Systems division was developing [[Autonomous Navigation System|autonomous navigation]] for the Stryker and several other vehicles with a $237 million contract, until the program was cut in July 2011.{{cite web |url=http://www.gdrs.com/programs/program.asp?UniqueID=22 |title=Autonomous Navigation System (ANS) |access-date=27 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131214101922/http://www.gdrs.com/programs/program.asp?UniqueID=22 |archive-date=14 December 2013 |url-status=dead}} The [[Tank Automotive Research, Development and Engineering Center]] (TARDEC) has tested an active [[magneto rheological suspension]], developed by [[MillenWorks]] for the Stryker, at the [[Yuma Proving Ground]], which resulted in greater vehicle stability.{{Cite web |url=http://www.millenworks.com/html/aboutus/news/Stryker_Test.pdf |title=Suspension test report, MillenWorks |access-date=16 October 2007 |archive-date=29 November 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071129094359/http://www.millenworks.com/html/aboutus/news/Stryker_Test.pdf |url-status=live}} In 2011, over 1,000 Stryker vehicles had been rebuilt by the [[Anniston Army Depot]] and returned to operations.Bacchus, Jennifer. [https://www.army.mil/article/69742/Anniston_Army_Depot_resets_1_000th_Stryker/ "Anniston Army Depot resets 1,000th Stryker."] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120720070649/http://www.army.mil/article/69742/Anniston_Army_Depot_resets_1_000th_Stryker |date=20 July 2012}} U.S. Army, 22 November 2011. ===Upgrades=== [[File:Fort Irwin National Training Center - Stryker - 4.jpg|thumb|A Stryker at [[Fort Irwin National Training Center]]]] Throughout its years in service, the Stryker has undergone various survivability upgrades and received "kit" applications designed to improve the vehicle's ability to withstand attacks.{{Citation|last=Osborn|first=Chris|title=Army marks 10-year Stryker anniversary|url=https://www.army.mil/article/56202/Army_marks_10_year_Stryker_anniversary/|year=2011|publisher=US Department of the Army|access-date=13 November 2017|archive-date=14 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171114093403/https://www.army.mil/article/56202/Army_marks_10_year_Stryker_anniversary/|url-status=live}} The US Army plans to improve its fleet of Stryker vehicles with the introduction of improved [[Active suspension|semi-active suspension]], modifications reshaping the hull into a shallow [[V-hull|V-shaped structure]], to protect against [[improvised explosive device]]s (IEDs). Included are additional armor for the sides, redesigned hatches to minimize gaps in the armor, blast-absorbent, mine-resistant seating, non-flammable tires, an upgrade to the remote weapon station that allows it to fire while moving, increased 500 ampere electrical generation, a new solid-state power distribution system and data bus, and the automotive and power plant systems improvements to support one-fourth greater gross vehicle weight. The upgraded V-hull will be part of the new StrykShield situational awareness kit, which will address many of these upgrades. [[Allegheny Technologies]]' ATI 500-MIL armor steel was designated the primary armored plating for the StrykShield package in 2008.{{Cite web|url=http://www.investquest.com/iq/a/ati/ne/news/ati100608.htm|title=U.S. Army Stryker Combat Vehicles to be Equipped with Allegheny Technologies' ATI 500-MIL Armor Steel}}{{Dead link|date=December 2021 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes}} The upgrade incorporating lessons learned from [[War in Afghanistan (2001–present)|combat in Afghanistan]] is designated LAV-H. In Afghanistan, it retained a 96 percent readiness rate. To upgrade the existing fleet, the Army has implemented an Engineering Change Proposal (ECP) program to provide a stronger engine, improved suspension, more onboard electrical power, and next-generation networking and computing technology. Phase 1 of the ECP includes an electrical power upgrade by replacing the extant 570 [[ampere|amp]] [[alternator]] with a higher current 910 amp alternator, replacing the existing 350 horsepower engine with a 450-horsepower engine, a stronger suspension system to improve mobility at higher weights, and an in-vehicle network to improve data and video sharing between crew stations and more secure and reliable data sharing between vehicle systems.[http://www.armyrecognition.com/august_2012_new_army_military_defence_industry_uk/united_states_army_plans_major_stryker_upgrads_with_ecp_engineering_change_proposal_program_0108124.html Stryker ECP upgrades] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203061009/http://www.armyrecognition.com/august_2012_new_army_military_defence_industry_uk/united_states_army_plans_major_stryker_upgrads_with_ecp_engineering_change_proposal_program_0108124.html |date=3 December 2013}} – Armyrecognition.com, 1 August 2012. In May 2013, Kongsberg Integrated Tactical Systems was awarded a contract to supply the Driver's Situational Awareness Display (DSAD) and Commander's Situational Awareness Display (CSAD) for the Stryker ECP program, featuring an onboard processor and additional [[I/O ports]] for both data and video.[https://web.archive.org/web/20130816041117/http://kongsberg.com/en/kps/news/2013/july/kongsberg%20awarded%20contract%20from%20gdls%20supporting%20us%20army%20stryker%20ecp%20program/ "KONGSBERG Awarded Contract from GDLS Supporting US Army Stryker ECP Program"] (press release), Kongsberg.com, 9 July 2013 As of January 2014, the U.S. Army had two Stryker Brigades that completed the DVH upgrade. A third brigade, the [[2nd Infantry Division (United States)|2nd Brigade, 2nd Infantry Division]] at [[Joint Base Lewis–McChord]], was to be fully upgraded by the end of FY 2016.[http://www.militarytimes.com/article/20140112/NEWS04/301120008/Army-plans-radical-upgrade-Stryker-brigades "Army plans radical upgrade of Stryker brigades"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140112154352/http://www.militarytimes.com/article/20140112/NEWS04/301120008/Army-plans-radical-upgrade-Stryker-brigades |date=12 January 2014}}, ''Military Times'', 12 January 2014. In mid-October 2014, the Army approved the procurement of DVH Strykers for a fourth Stryker brigade, with conversions to 360 vehicles to begin in FY 2017. The Strykers will be the first to receive ECPs to handle the upgrades better than the previous three brigade vehicles, which increased weight, decreased mobility, and added a power burden. Previous DVH-upgraded Strykers will get ECP enhancements when funding is available. ECP enhancements include a more robust 450 HP engine, a more powerful 910 amp power generator, a chassis upgrade to handle the new engine, and improvements to the vehicle's internal network.[http://www.armyrecognition.com/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=9634 Fourth brigade with enhanced Stryker combat vehicles planned for U.S. Army] – Armyrecognition.com, 14 October 2014 In 2018, the Army Requirements Oversight Council approved the conversion of all flat bottomed Strykers to the DVHA1 standard. This will be done through a combination of upgrading existing Strykers and new built vehicles. The Army acquisition goal for the fleet of DVHA1 vehicles is 4,459 which will allow all Stryker Brigades to field the vehicle and other units within the army which use the vehicle like M-SHORAD and CBRN detection. Procurement is to last into the 2030s with procurement averaging 165 Strykers a year or roughly half of a Stryker brigades vehicle set.{{Cite web |date=March 2023 |title=Justification Book Volume 1 of 1 Procurement of W&TCV, Army |url=https://www.asafm.army.mil/Portals/72/Documents/BudgetMaterial/2024/Base%20Budget/Procurement/Procurement%20of%20Weapons%20and%20Tracked%20Combat%20Vehicles.pdf }} Upgrading the fourth brigade also kept the production line active through 2018, whereas deciding to upgrade after the line had closed would be more difficult and costly to reopen it.[http://www.militarytimes.com/article/20141016/NEWS04/310160044/Army-waiting-Hill-OK-build-upgraded-Strykers "Army waiting for Hill OK to build upgraded Strykers"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141017003344/http://www.militarytimes.com/article/20141016/NEWS04/310160044/Army-waiting-Hill-OK-build-upgraded-Strykers |date=17 October 2014}}. ''Military Times'', 16 October 2014 The upgrades of the engine and power generator, {{cvt|60000|lb|abbr=on}} suspension, and DVH designate the vehicle the Stryker-A1.[https://www.armyrecognition.com/june_2018_global_defense_security_army_news_industry/us_army_awards_contract_to_general_dynamics_to_upgrade_strykers_to_a1_configuration.html "US Army awards contract to General Dynamics to upgrade Strykers to A1 configuration"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180630215546/https://www.armyrecognition.com/june_2018_global_defense_security_army_news_industry/us_army_awards_contract_to_general_dynamics_to_upgrade_strykers_to_a1_configuration.html |date=30 June 2018}}. ''Army Recognition''. 28 June 2018. The Army plans to increase the lethality of Stryker ICVs by having half equipped with a 30 mm cannon and the other half given a [[FGM-148|Javelin anti-tank missile]] on the existing [[Protector (RWS)|RWS]] in each brigade.[https://www.armytimes.com/story/defense/show-daily/ausa/2015/10/15/new-army-strategy-sees-future-combat-vehicles-as-highly-mobile-highly-lethal/73651700/ New Army Strategy Sees Future Combat Vehicles As Highly Mobile, Highly Lethal] – ''Army Times'', 15 October 2015 By September 2020, half of the 2nd Brigade, 4th Infantry Division had fielded the third-generation Stryker DVHA1 variant.[https://www.nationaldefensemagazine.org/articles/2020/9/18/army-begins-fielding-upgraded-third-generation-strykers Army Begins Fielding Upgraded Third-Generation Strykers] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200920045634/https://www.nationaldefensemagazine.org/articles/2020/9/18/army-begins-fielding-upgraded-third-generation-strykers |date=20 September 2020}}. ''National Defense Magazine''. 18 September 2020. ===M-SHORAD=== {{anchor|SHORAD}} {{commons category|Stryker M-SHORAD}} [[File:5-4 ADA train with Polish ADA during Saber Strike 2022 03.jpg|thumb|5th Battalion, [[4th Air Defense Artillery Regiment]], train with Maneuver Short Range Air Defense platform (M-SHORAD) prototypes during a training exercise at BPTA, Poland, February 2022]] In February 2018, the Army announced that Stryker vehicles would be modified with sensors and weapons to fulfill an interim Maneuver-Short-Range Air Defense (M-SHORAD) requirement. This is in response to a capability gap identified in Europe against Russian [[unmanned aerial vehicle]]s (UAVs). With the previous focus on fighting in the Middle East, the U.S. Army had neglected SHORAD capabilities.{{cite web |last1=Jr |first1=Sydney J. Freedberg |title=Army Fields First Anti-Aircraft Strykers In Just 3 Years |url=https://breakingdefense.com/2021/04/army-fields-first-anti-aircraft-strykers-in-only-3-years/ |website=Breaking Defense |date=23 April 2021}} In future conflicts, it is feared they would not be able to rely on air dominance to counter enemy aircraft. In addition to deploying [[AN/TWQ-1 Avenger]]s and fielding man-portable [[Stinger missile]]s, Strykers are to be upgraded to buy time to build a lasting mobile air defense solution.[https://www.militarytimes.com/land/2018/03/01/interim-short-range-air-defense-solution-will-be-stryker-based/ Interim short-range air defense solution to be Stryker-based] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180302181628/https://www.militarytimes.com/land/2018/03/01/interim-short-range-air-defense-solution-will-be-stryker-based/ |date=2 March 2018}}. ''Military Times''. 1 March 2018. Because the unarmored Humvee-based Avenger lacks survivability and range to keep up with maneuver forces and hold off enemy aircraft in contested territory, four battalions totaling 144 Stryker SHORADs are planned, with the first battery of 12 systems fielded in 2020. The Stryker platform was chosen because it has better protection and in regards to size, weight and power considerations, especially for the possibility of integrating a [[directed energy weapon]] in the future. The first unit to be equipped with them will be the 4th Battalion, [[5th Air Defense Artillery Regiment]]. The Army planned to select the weapons configuration to be fitted onto the vehicle in late 2018.[https://www.defensenews.com/land/2018/03/19/short-range-air-defense-interim-solution-to-be-chosen-by-end-of-year/ Interim solution for US Army's Short Range Air Defense to be chosen by end of year]. ''Defense News''. 19 March 2018. In June 2018, the Army chose [[Leonardo DRS]] to supply the mission equipment package, which partnered with [[Moog Inc.]] to integrate the Reconfigurable Integrated-weapons Platform (RIwP) onto the vehicle. The system can be fitted with a Stinger pod and [[AGM-114|Longbow Hellfire]] missile rails and comes equipped with a 30 mm [[M230 chain gun#M230LF and MAWS|M230LF chain gun]] and the 7.62 mm [[M240 machine gun|M240 coaxial machine gun]], as well as non-kinetic defeat capabilities and a [[RADA Electronic Industries]] onboard Multi-Mission Hemispheric Radar (MHR).[https://www.defensenews.com/land/2018/06/28/us-armys-interim-short-range-air-defense-solution-crystallizes/ US Army's interim short-range air defense solution crystallizes]. ''Defense News''. 29 June 2018. The Army chose DRS because of the flexibility of the reconfigurable turret to allow for growth opportunities and alternate weapon options. It posed less intrusion to the existing vehicle platform, as they have a desire to keep the Stryker as common across the fleet as possible, and it provided increased protection as the crew can reload ammunition under armor. All 144 M-SHORAD systems are planned to be delivered by 2022.[https://www.defensenews.com/land/2018/06/28/us-armys-interim-short-range-air-defense-solution-crystallizes/ US Army's interim short-range air defense solution crystallizes]. ''Defense News'', 29 June 2018. The turret can mount one four-shot Stinger pod or two Hellfire missiles on either side. Reloading of the M230LF and Stingers can be done through roof hatches giving partial protection. The system can act in a secondary anti-vehicle role, as the 30 mm cannon is larger than the 25 mm gun mounted on the M2 Bradley and the Hellfire has greater range than TOW missiles typically used by ground vehicles.[https://breakingdefense.com/2018/07/army-anti-aircraft-stryker-can-kill-tanks-too/ Army Anti-Aircraft Stryker Can Kill Tanks Too] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308022158/https://breakingdefense.com/2018/07/army-anti-aircraft-stryker-can-kill-tanks-too/ |date=8 March 2021}}. ''Breaking Defense''. 10 July 2018. In September 2020, the Army awarded General Dynamics the IM-SHORAD contract worth $1.2 billion, to deliver 144 vehicles over five years. The first order was for 28 vehicles for $230 million.[https://breakingdefense.com/2020/10/gdls-gets-1-2b-for-144-army-anti-aircraft-strykers/ GDLS Gets $1.2B For 144 Army Anti-Aircraft Strykers] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201004062714/https://breakingdefense.com/2020/10/gdls-gets-1-2b-for-144-army-anti-aircraft-strykers/ |date=4 October 2020}}. ''Breaking Defense''. 1 October 2020. The first four Stryker M-SHORAD vehicles were deployed to Germany in April 2021 as part of the 5th Battalion, 4th Air Defense Artillery Regiment under the [[10th Army Air and Missile Defense Command]]. A full battalion will be fielded in September 2021.[https://www.defensenews.com/land/2021/04/23/first-short-range-air-defense-systems-deploy-to-europe/ First short-range air defense systems deploy to Europe] {{Webarchive|url=http://webarchive.loc.gov/all/20210426210419/https://www.defensenews.com/land/2021/04/23/first%2Dshort%2Drange%2Dair%2Ddefense%2Dsystems%2Ddeploy%2Dto%2Deurope/ |date=26 April 2021}}. ''[[Defense News]]''. 23 April 2021.[https://breakingdefense.com/2021/04/army-fields-first-anti-aircraft-strykers-in-only-3-years/ Army Fields First Anti-Aircraft Strykers In Just 3 Years] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210425185310/https://breakingdefense.com/2021/04/army-fields-first-anti-aircraft-strykers-in-only-3-years/ |date=25 April 2021}}. ''Breaking Defense''. 23 April 2021. In 2024, the M-SHORAD [[air defense vehicle]] based on the Stryker platform was officially named the Sergeant Stout after the only Air Defense Artillery Soldier to receive the [[Medal of Honor]], [[Mitchell W. Stout]].{{cite web | url=https://www.army.mil/article/277291/army_names_the_m_shorad_after_vietnam_war_medal_of_honor_recipient | title=Army names the M-SHORAD after Vietnam War Medal of Honor recipient | date=15 June 2024 }} [[File:M-SHORAD Stryker.jpg|thumb|M-SHORAD with two [[Stinger missile]] pods]] As of 2025, the U.S. Army is advancing toward the M-SHORAD Increment 3 configuration to address operational shortcomings and counter increasingly complex aerial threats. A major update includes the planned removal of the AGM-114L Longbow Hellfire missiles from future variants. Mounted externally on the Stryker chassis, the Hellfires were subjected to constant vibration, environmental exposure, and rough terrain, which led to wear and tear on the missiles and raised safety concerns. To replace them, the Army is doubling the Stinger missile loadout from four to eight per vehicle by adding a second four-round pod. This expanded missile capacity enhances the system’s endurance in swarm or multi-axis engagements. The Stinger remains effective against rotary-wing aircraft and small UAVs but faces growing limitations against faster, higher-flying, or more maneuverable threats. To further improve capability, Increment 3 will introduce the Next Generation Short Range Interceptor (NGSRI), equipped with multi-mode seekers and an extended intercept range compared to the FIM-92 Stinger.{{Cite web |last=Congressional Research Service |date=13 August 2024 |title=U.S. Army's Maneuver Short-Range Air Defense System |url=https://sgp.fas.org/crs/weapons/IF12397.pdf |access-date=15 June 2025}}{{Cite web |title=RTX's Raytheon completes 10 subsystem demonstrations for U.S. Army's Next-Generation Short-Range Interceptor program |url=https://www.rtx.com/news/news-center/2025/02/18/rtxs-raytheon-completes-10-subsystem-demonstrations-for-u-s-armys-next-generat |access-date=2025-06-15 |website=United Technologies |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Trevithick |first=Joseph |date=2025-05-28 |title=Everything We Learned About Lockheed's QuadStar Missile Aimed At Replacing FIM-92 Stingers |url=https://www.twz.com/land/everything-we-learned-about-lockheeds-quadstar-missile-aimed-at-replacing-fim-92-stingers |access-date=2025-06-15 |website=The War Zone |language=en-US}} ====DE M-SHORAD==== [[File:Stryker DE M-SHORAD.jpg|thumb|DE M-SHORAD]] The Army began an effort to put a laser on an M-SHORAD vehicle during 2019.[https://www.defensenews.com/land/2023/04/13/army-short-range-air-defense-laser-prototypes-take-down-drones-at-yuma/ Army short-range air defense laser prototypes take down drones at Yuma]. ''[[Defense News]]''. 13 April 2023. A combat shoot-off of laser-equipped Strykers facing realistic scenarios was conducted in July 2021,[https://www.army.mil/article/249239/army_advances_first_laser_weapon_through_combat_shoot_off Army advances first laser weapon through Combat Shoot-Off] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210823202056/https://www.army.mil/article/249239/army_advances_first_laser_weapon_through_combat_shoot_off |date=23 August 2021}}. ''[[Army.mil]]''. 10 August 2021. after which [[Raytheon]] was awarded a contract to supply a platoon of four vehicles each equipped with a 50 kW laser to defend against [[U.S. military UAS groups|Group 1-3 UAS]] and rocket, artillery, and mortar (RAM) threats. The first two [[directed energy weapon|Directed Energy]] Maneuver-SHORAD Strykers were delivered in early 2023 for training with soldiers. A second platoon is planned to be ordered later in 2023, with the program to transfer to a program of record in 2025 and a competition to open up to produce the DE M-SHORAD capability. Four DE M-SHORAD Strykers were deployed to the Middle East in February 2024 for real-world testing.[https://breakingdefense.com/2024/03/exclusive-strykers-with-50-kilowatt-lasers-in-centcom-for-experiment-army-no-2-says/ EXCLUSIVE: Strykers with 50-kilowatt lasers in CENTCOM for experiment, Army No. 2 says]. ''Breaking Defense''. 1 March 2024. === TEWS === [[File:Tactical Electronic Warfare System (TEWS) Stryker.jpg|thumb|Tactical Electronic Warfare System (TEWS)]] The Tactical Electronic Warfare System (TEWS) is a tactical electronic warfare and signals intelligence variant integrated onto the Stryker combat vehicle for use by U.S. Army Brigade Combat Teams. TEWS is an all-weather, 24-hour mounted system fielded as a Quick Reaction Capability that provides electronic support and electronic attack against enemy radio frequency emitters. Each system consists of an integrated suite of antennas, receivers, processors, and electronic attack hardware installed on the Stryker, enabling operations while stationary or on the move. TEWS incorporates machine learning–based signal recognition, integrates Intelligence Community signal detectors and electronic attack techniques, and relies on GPS and tactical radio communications to support battlefield awareness and responsiveness.{{Cite web |last=General Dynamics Mission Systems |title=Tactical Electronic Warfare System (TEWS) |url=https://gdmissionsystems.com/-/media/general-dynamics/space-and-intelligence-systems/pdf/tactical-electronic-warfare-system-tews-datasheet.ashx |access-date=9 January 2026 |website=gdmissionsystems.com}}{{Cite web |date=2022-12-14 |title=PM EW&C - CPE IEW&S |url=https://peoiews.army.mil/pm-ewc/,%20https://peoiews.army.mil/pm-ewc/ |access-date=2026-01-09 |language=en-US}} ==Design== [[File:US Army 53413 Range Training in India fires up Strykehorse Soldiers.jpg|thumb|A view into the rear compartment]] The Stryker is based on the [[LAV III]] light armored vehicle, which was based on the [[LAV-25]] series. The vehicle comes in several variants with a common engine, transmission, hydraulics, wheels, tires, differentials and transfer case. The [[M1130 command vehicle]] and [[M1133 medical evacuation vehicle]] have an air conditioning unit mounted on the back. The medical vehicle has a higher-capacity generator. A recent upgrade program provided a field retrofit kit to add air conditioning units to all variants. Production started in 2005 on the Mobile Gun System, mounting an overhead General Dynamics Land Systems (GDLS) 105 mm automatic gun called the [[M1128 mobile gun system]].{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}} ===Engine and mechanical features=== For its [[powerpack (drivetrain)|powerpack]] the Stryker uses a [[Caterpillar Inc.|Caterpillar]] diesel engine common in U.S. Army medium-lift trucks, eliminating additional training for maintenance crews and allowing the use of common parts.{{citation needed|date=October 2023}} Because of obsolescence concerns, the [[Caterpillar 3126]] engine was recently replaced by a Caterpillar C7 engine and the Allison 3200SP transmission.[http://defense-update.com/newscast/0508/news/news1505_stryker.htm US Army Outlines Future Improvements for the Stryker] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180206030524/http://defense-update.com/newscast/0508/news/news1505_stryker.htm |date=6 February 2018}}. defense-update.com Pneumatic or hydraulic systems drive almost all of the vehicle's mechanical features. For example, a pneumatic system switches between 8×4 and 8×8 drive.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}} Designers strove to ease the maintainer's job, equipping most cables, hoses, and mechanical systems with quick-disconnecting mechanisms. The engine and transmission can be removed and reinstalled in approximately two hours, allowing repairs to the turbocharger and many other components to be done outside the vehicle.{{Citation needed|date=May 2010}} ===Command, control, and targeting=== [[File:Rws stryker interiorscreen.jpg|thumb|A [[remote weapon system]] screen]] Extensive computer support helps soldiers fight the enemy while reducing [[friendly fire]] incidents. Each vehicle can track friendly vehicles in the field as well as detected enemies. The driver and the vehicle commander, who also serves as the gunner, have [[periscope]]s that allow them to see outside the vehicle without exposing themselves to outside dangers. The vehicle commander has access to a day-night [[thermal imaging]] camera which allows the vehicle commander to see what the driver sees. The vehicle commander has an almost 360-degree field of vision.{{Cite web |title=TC 7-21 Chapter 6 |url=https://rdl.train.army.mil/catalog-ws/view/100.ATSC/BE842D10-198F-4595-8032-6E26C30A9284-1274577722006/7-21/chap6.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230527150927/https://rdl.train.army.mil/catalog-ws/view/100.ATSC/BE842D10-198F-4595-8032-6E26C30A9284-1274577722006/7-21/chap6.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=27 May 2023 |access-date=2025-01-31 |website=rdl.train.army.mil}} The Stryker vehicle is equipped with advanced camera systems to enhance driver visibility in various conditions. The AN/VAS–5 Driver’s Vision Enhancer (DVE), a compact thermal camera with a high-resolution infrared sensor, provides a 50-degree field of view for effective navigation in low-visibility environments such as fog, smoke, and dust.{{Cite web |last=Department of Defense |date=24 October 2024 |title=Notice of Proposed Issuance of Letter of Offer Pursuant to Section 36(b)(1) of the Arms Export Control Act |url=https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2024-25117.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250131182537/https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2024-25117.pdf |archive-date=31 January 2025 |access-date=31 January 2025}} On the [[M1296 Dragoon|M1296 Infantry Carrier Vehicle Dragoon (ICV-D)]], this system has been replaced by the DVE-Wide, which provides a 107-degree horizontal field of view.{{Cite web |title=Driver's Vision Enhancer Wide (DVE Wide) |url=https://www.leonardodrs.com/what-we-do/products-and-services/driver-s-vision-enhancer-wide-dve-wide/ |access-date=2025-02-01 |website=Leonardo DRS |language=en-US}} The DVE-Wide |url=https://breakingdefense.com/2018/10/general-dynamics-upgrades-the-upgunned-stryker-for-the-army/ |access-date=2025-02-01 |website=Breaking Defense |language=en-US}} Both systems feature image stabilization to counteract shock and vibration, while their ruggedized displays ensure reliability in demanding tactical environments.{{Cite web |last=U.S. Senate |date=5 September 2023 |title=CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — SENATE |url=https://www.congress.gov/118/crec/2023/09/05/169/142/CREC-2023-09-05-pt1-PgS3884.pdf |url-status=live 2025}} The [[United States Army|U.S. Army]] is also working to integrate the DVE-Wide cameras on the Stryker with the [[Integrated Visual Augmentation System]] (IVAS) to give the crew and dismounts a training with the vehicles from computer training modules inside the vehicle. This capability allows the vehicle to warn dismounted soldiers of threats which lie beyond the range of their night vision sights.[http://www.popularmechanics.com/military/a2696/4253991/ "Stryker Crews in Iraq Rally to Defend Their Rides: Field Report"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150527052424/http://www.popularmechanics.com/military/a2696/4253991/ |date=27 May 2015}}. Popularmechanics.com, 30 September 2009 ===Protection=== [[File:Stryker vehicle from the 56th SBCT.jpg|thumb|A Stryker with slat armor, full Hull Protection Kit and commander's ballistic shield]] The Stryker's hull is constructed from high-hardness steel which offers a basic level of protection against [[14.5×114mm|14.5]] mm rounds on the frontal arc. It has all-around protection against 7.62 mm ball ammunition. Strykers are equipped with bolt-on ceramic armor which offers all-around protection against 14.5 mm armor-piercing ammunition, and artillery fragments from 155 mm rounds.{{cite news |url=http://www4.army.mil/ocpa/read.php?story_id_key=965 |title=Stryker gets new armor, decreases in weight |author=Staff Sgt. Marcia Triggs |publisher=US Army |date=9 March 2002 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040623011941/http://www4.army.mil/ocpa/read.php?story_id_key=965 |archive-date=23 June 2004}} Problems were encountered with the initial batch of ceramic armor when it was found that a number of panels failed in tests against 14.5 mm ammunition. Army officials determined that this was due to changes in the composition and size of the panels introduced by their manufacturer, [[IBD Deisenroth Engineering|IBD Deisenroth]]. A stopgap solution of adding another 3 mm of steel armor was introduced until a permanent solution could be found.{{cite news |url=https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/20030916/stryker16m/some-stryker-tiles-fail-under-fire-maker-rushes-to-fortify-vehicles |title=Some Stryker tiles fail under fire Maker rushes to fortify vehicles before deployment |author1=Ray Rivera |author2=Hal Bernton |work=Seattle Times |date=16 September 2003 |access-date=18 May 2010 |archive-date=28 September 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120928113023/http://community.seattletimes.nwsource.com/archive/?date=20030916&slug=stryker16m |url-status=live}} The issue was resolved in 2003 when DEW Engineering was selected as the new, exclusive supplier for the ceramic armor.{{cite press release |url=http://www.dewengineering.com/update051109/news.htm#GDLS-C |title=GDLS-C provides $39.5 Million order to DEW for Stryker Armour |date=15 January 2010 |publisher=DEW Engineering}} [[File:Buried IED blast in 2007 in Iraq.jpg|thumb|A Stryker rolled over by a buried IED in Iraq. All crew survived, but the vehicle required a factory rebuild before returning to service, 2007.{{citation |first=SPC. Lindsey M. |last=Bradford |url=https://www.army.mil/article/9708/general-lee-rides-again/ |title=General Lee rides again |publisher=US Army |date=6 June 2008 |access-date=9 October 2010 |archive-date=14 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091114221304/http://www.army.mil/-news/2008/06/06/9708-general-lee-rides-again/ |url-status=live}}]] In addition to the integral ceramic armor, optional packages have been developed. These include [[slat armor]]{{cite web |url=http://www.defense-update.com/products/s/slat-stryker.htm |title=Slat Armour for Stryker |publisher=defense-update.com |access-date=29 March 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120130013026/http://www.defense-update.com/products/s/slat-stryker.htm |archive-date=30 January 2012 |url-status=dead}} and Stryker [[reactive armor]] tiles (SRAT) for protection against rocket propelled grenades and other projectiles, the hull protection kit (HPK), armored skirts for additional protection against improvised explosive devices, and a ballistic shield to protect the commander's hatch. The Army began sending reactive armor tiles to Strykers in Iraq in 2004, as well as tiles for Abrams tanks and Bradley Fighting Vehicles. Tiles have to be specifically crafted for each vehicle type they are fitted to. Insurgents attempted to counter reactive armor by having teams fire multiple RPGs at once, but at close range these groups could be engaged and broken up. Reactive armor can be defeated by tandem-charge weapons like the [[RPG-29]] or by [[explosively formed penetrator]]s, although the Bradley's tiles can withstand EFPs.[https://archive.today/20140715031220/http://www.armytimes.com/article/20070413/NEWS/704130334/Army-officials-tout-success-reactive-armor "Army officials tout success of reactive armor"] ''Army Times'', 13 April 2007 In 2005, slat armor for the Stryker vehicles was designed and developed by the [[United States Army Research Laboratory|Army Research Laboratory]] and the Aberdeen Test Center in Maryland to further protect them from RPGs.{{cite journal|last=Rooney|first=John|date=January 2007 |title=Armor Testing, An Example of T&E for Rapid Acquisitions |url=http://www.dtic.mil/docs/citations/ADA519230|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210310001640/http://www.dtic.mil/docs/citations/ADA519230|url-status=dead|archive-date=10 March 2021|journal=ITEA Journal|pages=4–6|via=Defense Technical Information Center}} The cage is placed 50 cm ahead around the vehicle to provide adequate protection.{{cite thesis|last=Yap|first=Chun|date=September 2012|title=The Impact of Armor on the Design, Utilization and Survivability of Ground Vehicles: The History of Armor Development and Use|url=http://www.dtic.mil/docs/citations/ADA567418|journal=Naval Postgraduate School|via=Defense Technical Information Center|hdl=10945/17482|hdl-access=free|access-date=28 June 2018|archive-date=11 June 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170611171354/http://www.dtic.mil/docs/citations/ADA567418|url-status=dead}} The slat armor on the Stryker vehicles is effective against HEAT rounds. In May 2009, General Dynamics and [[Rafael Advanced Defense Systems|Rafael]] won a contract to provide SRAT tiles to replace slat armor on Strykers. The additional weight of the two systems is comparable, but reactive armor tiles offer greater vehicle stability and maneuverability and "assured" rather than "statistical" protection.[http://defense-update.com/features/2009/may/stryker_reactive_270509.html General Dynamics, Rafael to Replace the Strykers' SLAT Protection Cages with Reactive Armor] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180204225904/http://defense-update.com/features/2009/may/stryker_reactive_270509.html |date=4 February 2018}} – Defense-Update.com, 27 May 2009 The Stryker incorporates an [[Fire suppression system|automatic fire-extinguishing system]] with [[sensor]]s in the engine and troop compartments that activate one or more [[Halomethane|halon]] fire bottles, which can also be activated by the driver, externally mounted fuel tanks, and a [[NBC (weapon)|CBRN]] (Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear) Warfare system which will keep the crew compartment airtight and positively pressurized.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}} Reports from military personnel and analysts state that the Stryker's is better able to survive IEDs than other light military vehicles.{{cite web |url=http://www.fit.edu/fip/documents/SecNews1.pdf |archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20070926043803/http://www.fit.edu/fip/documents/SecNews1.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=26 September 2007 |title=Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) in Iraq and Afghanistan: Effects and Countermeasures, Congressional Research Service |date=25 September 2006 |author=Clay Wilson |publisher=[[Library of Congress]] |access-date=8 January 2007}}[http://www.blackanthem.com/News/U_S_Military_19/Stryker_increases_troops_survivability3281.shtml "Stryker increases troops' survivability"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716191000/http://www.blackanthem.com/News/U_S_Military_19/Stryker_increases_troops_survivability3281.shtml |date=16 July 2011}}. Both rounds are vital upgrades for the U.S. Army’s Stryker Brigade Combat Teams.{{Cite web |last=LTC Paul Santamaria |date=19 September 2022 |title=Future Force Capabilities |url=https://ndia.dtic.mil/wp-content/uploads/2022/future/Tues_GM_PMMAS_Santamaria.pdf |access-date=26 January 2025}}{{Cite web |date=2024-10-09 |title=Medium Caliber Product Office awards $78.5M contract for 30mm Airburst Ammunition |url=https://www.army.mil/article/280331/medium_caliber_product_office_awards_78_5m_contract_for_30mm_airburst_ammunition |access-date=2025-01-26 |website=www.army.mil |language=en}} ===Mobility=== ====Strategic and operational==== [[File:Stryker MC unloading from C130.jpg|thumb|A Stryker unloading from a [[C-130]]]] One of the key objectives outlined as part of the Army transformation plan was the ability to deploy a brigade anywhere in the world within 96 hours, a division in 120 hours, and five divisions within 30 days. Operational mobility requirements dictated that the vehicle be transportable by [[C-130]] aircraft and that it would be able to roll-off manned and ready to fight. The Stryker's suitability for C-130 transport has led to criticism that the aircraft's range may not meet the 1,000-mile goal. The aircraft's range depends on variables such as the C-130 variant and conditions at the departure airport.{{cite web |url=http://www.gao.gov/new.items/d04925.pdf |title=Fielding of Army's Stryker Vehicles Is Well Under Way, but Expectations for Their Transportability by C-130 Aircraft Need to Be Clarified |date=August 2004 |publisher=GAO |access-date=9 August 2004 |archive-date=27 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140327044426/http://www.gao.gov/new.items/d04925.pdf |url-status=live}} In a demonstration conducted in April 2003, a Stryker infantry company with 21 Stryker vehicles was transported by C-130s to another airport 70 miles away. This proved that the vehicle can be transported by C-130, but did not address the concerns regarding range and airport departure conditions. When equipped with [[slat armor]] the Stryker is too large to fit on a C-130, but [[Rocket-propelled grenade|RPG]] protection was not a requirement for C-130 transport. The [[Airbus A400M Atlas]] was being tested for compatibility with the Stryker in Autumn 2015.{{Cite web | url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/raf-a400m-stretches-legs-on-us-detachment-417161/ | title=RAF A400M stretches legs on US detachment | access-date=28 September 2015 | archive-date=29 September 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150929125211/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/raf-a400m-stretches-legs-on-us-detachment-417161/ | url-status=live}} The Stryker is too heavy, 19–26 tons, depending on variant and add-on features, to be lifted by existing helicopters. In August 2004, testing was conducted to determine if the Stryker MGS could be airdropped. This testing started with a series of 12-foot drop tests, followed by the [[United States Air Force|US Air Force]] successfully airdropping an up-weighted Stryker Engineering Support Vehicle from a [[Boeing C-17 Globemaster III|C-17]].{{citation needed|date=October 2023}} Even though this test was a success, none of the Stryker variants have been certified for airdrop. As of 2013 work continues in this area with the capability assumed for the Unified Quest war game.{{cite web |url=http://www.defensenews.com/article/20130331/DEFREG02/303310003/War-Game-Exposes-Gaps-U-S-Army |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130410175502/http://www.defensenews.com/article/20130331/DEFREG02/303310003/War-Game-Exposes-Gaps-U-S-Army |url-status=dead |archive-date=10 April 2013 |title=War Game Exposes Gaps for U.S. Army|work=Defense News|access-date=24 December 2014}} ====Tactical==== The Stryker can alter the pressure in all eight tires to suit terrain conditions: highway, cross-country, mud/sand/snow, and emergency. The system warns the driver if the vehicle exceeds the recommended speed for its tire pressure, then automatically inflates the tires to the next higher pressure setting. The system can warn the driver of a flat tire. The Stryker is equipped with [[run-flat tire]] inserts that also serve as [[beadlock|bead-locks]], allowing the vehicle to move at reduced speeds for several miles before the tire completely deteriorates.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}} [[File:US Army 53414 Range Training in India fires up Strykehorse Soldiers.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|U.S. Army and [[Indian Army]] troops with a Stryker IFV during a bilateral training exercise]] Some criticism of the Stryker continues a decades-long ongoing debate concerning whether tracked or wheeled vehicles are more effective.{{cite journal |url=https://fas.org/man/dod-101/sys/land/docs/2wheels98.pdf |title=The Wheel versus Track dilemma |journal=[[Armor (magazine)|Armor]] |author=Paul Hornback |date=March–April 1998 |pages=33–34 |access-date=25 November 2015 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304103948/http://fas.org/man/dod-101/sys/land/docs/2wheels98.pdf |url-status=live}} Conventional tracks have superior off-road mobility, greater load capacity, can pivot a vehicle in place, and are more resistant to battle damage. Wheeled vehicles are easier to maintain, and have higher road speeds. The US Army chose the Stryker over tracked vehicles due to these advantages.{{cite web |url=http://archive.gao.gov/legald425p10/a00952.pdf |title=GAO Denies protest in choosing the Stryker over the M113 and M8 |access-date=13 July 2008 |work=GAO |archive-date=11 August 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110811184748/http://archive.gao.gov/legald425p10/a00952.pdf |url-status=live}} [[Vehicle rollover|Rollover]] is a greater risk with the Stryker relative to other transport vehicles, due to its higher [[center of gravity]]. The Stryker's high [[ground clearance]], however, is likely to reduce the damage caused by land mines and [[improvised explosive device|IED]]s on the vehicle.{{cite press release |url=http://www.gdels.com/descargas/ELS_Press%20Release_PIRANHAv2.pdf |title=GDELS briefs on evaluation of the PIRANHA armoured wheeled vehicle system at EUROSATORY 2008 |publisher=[[General Dynamics]] European Land Systems |page=2 |date=16 June 2008 |access-date=16 May 2010 |archive-date=11 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110711081417/http://www.gdels.com/descargas/ELS_Press%20Release_PIRANHAv2.pdf |url-status=live}} While not amphibious, the Stryker has watertight combat hatch seals to allow [[ford (crossing)|fording]] water up to the tops of its wheels.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}} ===Cost=== The unit cost to purchase the initial Stryker ICVs, without add-ons, including the slat armor, was US$3 million in April 2002.{{citation needed|date=January 2022}} By May 2003, the regular production cost per vehicle was US$1.42 million.{{cite web |url=http://www.gao.gov/new.items/d03671.pdf |title=GAO Compares Stryker to M113A3 |access-date=13 July 2008 |work=GAO |page=20 |archive-date=24 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924045244/http://www.gao.gov/new.items/d03671.pdf |url-status=live}} In February 2012, the cost had risen to US$4.9 million. In 2013, media reports stated that the Stryker Project Management Office had ordered almost $900 million in unneeded or outdated parts due to a failure to control its inventory during the [[war on terror]].{{cite news|author=Ashton, Adam|date=2 April 2013|title=DOD Inspector General finds $900M stockpile of Stryker parts|work=Stars and Stripes|url=http://www.stripes.com/news/army/dod-inspector-general-finds-900m-stockpile-of-stryker-parts-1.214680|access-date=7 December 2013|archive-date=11 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131211102319/http://www.stripes.com/news/army/dod-inspector-general-finds-900m-stockpile-of-stryker-parts-1.214680|url-status=live}}[http://www.thenewstribune.com/2013/07/22/2688974/stryker-audit-finds-muddy-repair.htm "Stryker audit finds muddy repair spending."] {{Dead link|date=December 2018|bot=InternetArchiveBot|fix-attempted=yes}}. ''The News Tribune'', 22 July 2013. ===Mission=== [[File:US Navy 050320-N-9588P-027 U.S. Army Soldiers ploy out of the back of a Stryker infantry carrier vehicle to provide suppressive fire on the enemy during a simulated convoy attack.jpg|thumb|Members of the 1-23rd Infantry Regiment deploying from the rear ramp of a Stryker, 2005]] A standard Stryker Brigade typically consists of: 130 Infantry Carrier Vehicles; 9 Anti-Tank Guided Missile Vehicles; 27 Medical Evacuation Vehicles; 12 Engineer Squad Vehicles; 32 Commander's Vehicles; 36 120 mm Mounted Mortar Carriers; 56 Reconnaissance Vehicles; 13 Fire Support Vehicles; three NBC Reconnaissance Vehicles; and 12 105 mm Mobile Gun Systems. The Stryker family of vehicles fills a role in the United States Army that is neither heavy nor light, but rather an attempt to create a force that can move infantry to the battlefield quickly and in relative security. Brigades that have been converted to the Stryker have primarily been light, or, in the case of the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, unarmored [[Humvee]]-based cavalry scouts. For these units, the addition of Strykers has increased combat power by providing armor protection, a vehicle-borne weapon system to support each dismounted squad, and the speed and range to conduct missions far from the operating base.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}} Stryker units seem to be especially effective in urban areas, where vehicles can establish initial security positions near a building and dismount squads on a doorstep.{{Citation needed|date=October 2020}} The Stryker relies on its speed and communications for the majority of its defense against heavy weapon systems. Most Stryker variants are not designed to engage heavily armored units, relying on communication and other units to control threats outside of its classification. One variant is armed with anti-tank missiles.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}} Brigades equipped with the Stryker are intended to be strategically mobile, i.e., capable of being rapidly deployed over long distances. As such, the Stryker was intentionally designed with a lower level of protection compared to tracked vehicles like the M2 Bradley, but with much lower logistic requirements.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}} Although the Stryker was designed to be rapidly deployable and not heavily armored, a training exercise in January 2014 demonstrated that in some circumstances, a Stryker brigade with vehicles and infantry using anti-tank missiles could successfully engage a conventional enemy force of tanks, armored vehicles, and helicopters.[http://www.stripes.com/news/us/stryker-crews-find-ways-to-defeat-armored-enemy-1.268179 "Stryker crews find ways to defeat armored enemy"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222035641/http://www.stripes.com/news/us/stryker-crews-find-ways-to-defeat-armored-enemy-1.268179 |date=22 February 2014}}. Stripes.com, 17 February 2014.{{cite web |url=http://www.thenewstribune.com/2014/02/17/3051951/stryker-crews-find-ways-to-defeat.html |title=Stryker crews find ways to defeat armored enemy | Military News | The News Tribune |access-date=14 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140314221749/http://www.thenewstribune.com/2014/02/17/3051951/stryker-crews-find-ways-to-defeat.html |archive-date=14 March 2014 |url-status=dead}} ==Service history== ===Deployments=== [[File:Stryker 25th ID Iraq DF-SD-05-12693.JPEG|thumb|A M1126 Stryker ICV on patrol near [[Mosul]], Iraq, 2005]] * [[Iraq War]], 2003–2011: ** The first Stryker brigades were deployed to Iraq in October 2003. 3rd Brigade, 2nd Infantry Division from [[Fort Lewis (Washington)|Fort Lewis]] was the first to field and deploy the Stryker vehicle to combat in Iraq from November 2003 to November 2004. ** 3rd Brigade was relieved by 1st Brigade, 25th Infantry Division (SBCT). The main chassis is the [[Infantry fighting vehicle|infantry carrier vehicle]] (ICV). The Stryker vehicles have the following variants:{{cite web |url=http://www.sbct.army.mil/ |title=US Army SBCT Project Management Office |access-date=31 July 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060722174601/http://www.sbct.army.mil/ |archive-date=22 July 2006 |url-status=dead}} * [[M1126 infantry carrier vehicle]] (ICV): The basic armored personnel carrier version, which provides protected transport for two crew and a nine-man infantry squad, and can support dismounted infantry. It weighs 19 tons; communications include text and a [[map]] network between vehicles. It can be armed with 12.7 mm [[M2 Browning machine gun]], 40 mm [[Mk 19 grenade launcher]] or 7.62 mm [[M240 machine gun]]. ** M1126 infantry carrier vehicle DVH-Scout (ICVV-S): A reconnaissance version of the ICV fitted with an internally mounted long-range advance scout (LRAS) surveillance system and the double v-hull. * [[M1127 reconnaissance vehicle]] (RV): A version used by [[Reconnaissance, surveillance, and target acquisition (United States)|RSTA]] squadrons and battalion scouts. [[File:M1128 firing.jpg|thumb|M1128 MGS firing]] * [[M1128 mobile gun system]] (MGS): A version armed with an 105 mm [[M68 (tank gun)|M68A1E4]] rifled cannon, a 7.62 mm M240 machine gun mounted coaxially, a 12.7 mm M2 commander's machine gun and two M6 smoke grenade launchers. The M68A1E4 also features a [[muzzle brake]] to assist with recoil and an [[autoloader]]. The MGS vehicle is a strengthened variant of the [[LAV III]] compared to the standard variant other Stryker vehicles are based on, but retains commonality across all vehicles in the family. The Stryker MGS was retired at the end of 2022, due in part to the expense and difficulty of maintaining and upgrading the autoloader.{{Cite web |date=2021-05-12 |title=Army announces divestiture of the Stryker Mobile Gun System |url=https://www.army.mil/article/246274/army_announces_divestiture_of_the_stryker_mobile_gun_system |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241217222453/https://www.army.mil/article/246274/army_announces_divestiture_of_the_stryker_mobile_gun_system |archive-date=17 December 2024 |access-date=8 January 2025 |website=www.army.mil |language=en}} [[File:Stryker MCV-B.jpg|thumb|[[Soltam K6|120 mm]] mortar fired from Stryker MCV-B variant]] * [[M1129 mortar carrier]] (MC): armed with [[Soltam K6|Soltam 120 mm]] and [[Cardom]] recoil mortar system (RMS).{{Cite web |last=U.S. Army |date=February 2009 |title=Stryker Mortar Platoon and Section Leaders' Handbook |url=https://www.globalsecurity.org/military/library/policy/army/other/st3-22-7.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220122174319/https://www.globalsecurity.org/military/library/policy/army/other/st3-22-7.pdf |archive-date=22 January 2022 |access-date=8 January 2025}} * [[M1130 commander's vehicle]] (CV): This vehicle provides commanders with [[communication]], data, and control functions to analyze and prepare information for combat missions. They are deployed as three vehicles per brigade headquarters, two per battalion headquarters and two per infantry company. * [[M1131 fire support vehicle]] (FSV): This version is organic to maneuver companies and provides [[surveillance]] and communications (4 secure combat radio nets), with target acquisition/identification/tracking/designation being transmitted automatically to the shooting units. * [[M1132 engineer squad vehicle]] (ESV): This vehicle provides mobility and limited counter mobility support. [[File:Strykerinterior lg.jpg|thumb|Interior of medical evacuation vehicle]] * [[M1133 medical evacuation vehicle]] (MEV): This is used as the en route care platform for brigade units, part of the battalion aid station, providing treatment for serious injury and advanced trauma as an integrated part of the combat forward formation. [[File:Flickr - The U.S. Army - TOW missile fire.jpg|thumb|Anti-tank guided [[missile vehicle]] ]] * [[M1134 anti-tank guided missile vehicle]] (ATGM): It is a [[missile vehicle]] armed with the [[BGM-71 TOW|TOW]] missile to reinforce the brigade's infantry and reconnaissance, providing long-range anti-tank fires against armor beyond tank gun effective range. [[File:Comanche Troop hones gunnery skills - 210212-A-DQ632-0001 03.jpg|thumb|M1296 Dragoon]] * [[M1296 Dragoon]]: The Dragoon is the first variant of the Stryker family to be equipped as an Infantry Fighting Vehicle (IFV). Modifications were made to the hull roof of the Stryker for installing a Kongsberg unmanned turret with an [[Mk44 Bushmaster II#XM813|XM813]] 30 mm cannon, capable of firing airburst munitions.{{Cite web |date=2014-09-16 |title=30-mm weapon system on display |url=https://www.army.mil/article/133815/30_mm_weapon_system_on_display/ |access-date=2025-01-07 |website=www.army.mil |language=en}} This added around two tons of weight to the vehicle. Seven Stryker versions are being produced in this configuration: the M1256 ICVV, M1252 MCVV, M1255CVV, M1251 FSVV, M1257 ESVV, M1254 MEVV and M1253 ATVV. The M1127 reconnaissance vehicle, the M1128 mobile gun system and the M1135 NBC reconnaissance vehicle are not being produced in a double-V-hull configuration. The M1127 reconnaissance vehicle is to be replaced by a scout variant of the ICVV (called the ICVV-S), while the MGS version was divested in 2022.{{cite web |title=Project Manager Stryker Brigade Combat Team |url=http://www.peogcs.army.mil/documents/SBCT-Portfolio.pdf|access-date=9 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161020022445/https://www.peogcs.army.mil/documents/SBCT-Portfolio.pdf|archive-date=20 October 2016 |url-status=dead}} === Double V-hull A1 === The Double V-Hull A1 (DVH A1) is a modernized upgrade of the original Stryker Double V-Hull (DVH) variants, addressing key performance and capability needs. If the deal proceeds, first of the units will be directly imported while the rest will be co-produced in India and several changes will be also made in the platform to make it compatible in high-altitude terrain.{{Cite web |last=Deshpande |first=Smruti |date=2024-07-05 |title=India set to carry out trials for US-made Stryker combat vehicles in Ladakh & deserts |url=https://theprint.in/defence/india-set-to-carry-out-trials-for-us-made-stryker-combat-vehicles-in-ladakh-deserts/2160964/ |access-date=2024-07-06 |website=ThePrint |language=en-US}} As of October 2024, the discussions about the procurement has been paused.{{Cite news |last=Pubby |first=Manu |date=2024-10-16 |title=India's plan to buy Stryker armoured vehicles hits snag amid diplomatic rift with Canada |url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/defence/indias-plan-to-buy-stryker-armoured-vehicles-hits-snag-amid-diplomatic-rift-with-canada/articleshow/114292616.cms |access-date=2024-10-18 |work=The Economic Times |issn=0013-0389}}{{Cite news |date=2024-10-18 |title=India-Canada diplomatic row: Indian Army's plan to buy Ontario-produced Stryker armoured vehicles hits snag |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/business/india-business/india-canada-diplomatic-rift-indian-armys-plan-to-buy-ontario-produced-stryker-armoured-vehicles-hits-snag/articleshow/114308485.cms |access-date=2024-10-18 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}} On 10 January 2025, proposals to establish manufacturing for the Stryker in India were approved by the US government.{{cite web |last1=Sharma |first1=Ritu |title=India To Become 1st "Global Producer" Of Stryker Combat Vehicles; Locally Produce Sonobuoys For Anti-Sub Warfare |url=https://www.eurasiantimes.com/india-to-become-1st-global-producer/ |website=The EurAsian Times |access-date=2 February 2025 |date=January 10, 2025}} While Stryker initially did not meet Indian Army's needs, an amphibious variant of the vehicle is expected to be developed as of July 2025. In 2006, the [[Canadian Armed Forces|Canadian Forces]] asked its government to cancel the MGS acquisition. The MGS was originally intended to be used in the "Direct Fire Unit",{{cite web |url=http://www.army.forces.gc.ca/lf/English/5_4_1_4.asp |title=A Soldier's Guide to Army Transformation – Building a Direct Fire Unit |access-date=28 December 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080622091027/http://www.army.forces.gc.ca/lf/English/5_4_1_4.asp |archive-date=22 June 2008 |url-status=dead}} which will include [[TOW Under Armour|Tow Under Armour (LAV III)]] and [[Air Defense Anti-Tank System|MMEV (ADATS on LAV III)]]. The MGS was to provide the direct gun fire capabilities of the retiring [[Leopard 1#Canada|Leopard C2]] tank.{{Cite web |date=30 October 2003 |title=Mobile Gun System vs. Leopard tank |url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/background/cdnmilitary/equipment.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031031042623/http://www.cbc.ca/news/background/cdnmilitary/equipment.html |archive-date=31 October 2003 |website=cbc.ca}} With the recent demonstrated usefulness of tanks in Iraq and hurried deployment of Canadian Leopard C2 tanks to Afghanistan, Canada announced the purchase of surplus [[Leopard 2]]s from the [[Netherlands]].{{Cite web |last=Akin |first=David |date=31 October 2006 |title=Army might buy surplus tanks from Germans, Swiss |url=http://www.ctv.ca/servlet/ArticleNews/story/CTVNews/20061031/canada_tanks_061031/20061031?hub=Canada |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071014042154/http://www.ctv.ca/servlet/ArticleNews/story/CTVNews/20061031/canada_tanks_061031/20061031?hub=Canada |archive-date=14 October 2007 |website=ctv.ca}} The MMEV project has since been canceled, and the TUA requirement cut in half. ; {{flag|Israel}} : The [[Israel Defense Forces]] (IDF) had received three Stryker variants for trials, the first of which were vehicles from early production and did not include add-on armor.{{citation needed|date=October 2010}} A 2004 article in ''[[The Jerusalem Post]]'' cited an unnamed military source who said the deal was "buried for good", and speculated that the Stryker was not chosen due to a number of shortcomings. In 2008, the IDF began receiving the locally designed and produced [[Namer]] heavy armored personnel carriers instead.{{cite news |url=http://fr.jpost.com/servlet/Satellite?pagename=JPost/JPArticle/ShowFull&cid=1090208251924&p=1078027574121 |title=Stryker APC deal tabled for two years |date=19 July 2004 |work=Jerusalem Post |author=Arieh O'Sullivan |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090416220150/http://www.jpost.com/servlet/Satellite?pagename=JPost%2FJPArticle%2FShowFull |archive-date=16 April 2009 |access-date=31 August 2018 |url-status=dead}} ; {{flag|Lithuania}} : In 2015, the Lithuanian State Defence Council chose the German made [[Boxer (armoured fighting vehicle)|Boxer IFV]] over the US-made Stryker.
